title: Survival under Soviet rule
hook: while churches were shut, grandmothers kept faith alive in hidden prayer until churches reopened

segments.voice: Yesterday: Desmond Tutu, weeping at the table, then lifting his head to keep listening. Your line: truth, then reconciliation.

Don't tell your teacher. A grandmother says it softly, with a child on her knee, in a small apartment high in a gray block. In the corner, up where two walls meet, there's a little shelf with a painted icon and a tiny oil lamp. She has just taught the child to touch forehead, chest, one shoulder, the other, and to repeat a prayer after her, line by line. Don't tell anyone at school. The child nods, not really knowing why. This is how faith got through the years when the state wanted it gone.

In the Soviet Union, the state taught that religion would fade away, and it worked hard to help it fade. Churches were closed, and some were turned into warehouses, clubs or museums of atheism. Priests and bishops were arrested; some were shot, some sent to camps. Believers could lose a job or a place at university. And not only the Orthodox: Catholics, Lutherans and Baptists were pressed too, and so were Muslims and Jews. So who kept the faith alive? In many stories from those years, the grandmothers, the babushkas. Some say officials paid less attention to old women in headscarves. They had less to lose, and some were raising the children while the parents worked. They kept the icon corner. They baked the Easter bread. They taught the prayers in whispers. Some family stories tell of grandmothers quietly taking a baby to a priest to be baptized, without telling the parents. The Bible has this pattern too. A letter in Paul's name to his young friend Timothy remembers, in the King James Bible, "the unfeigned faith that is in thee, which dwelt first in thy grandmother Lois, and thy mother Eunice." Faith passed down a kitchen, not a lecture hall. When the Soviet system fell and churches reopened, grandmothers were among those standing inside, some in the same headscarves. Some of the young people who came in after them had first learned to cross themselves on a babushka's knee. The state had the schools, the newspapers and the police. The grandmothers had the corner shelf, and patience.

Bring to mind a grandmother, yours or someone else's, or any older person who passed something on to you: a recipe, a song, a prayer, a way of folding laundry, or of not giving up. Picture her hands doing it, and notice what of hers you still carry without thinking. Living or not, hold her with gratitude, and if you pray, thank God for her by name.
Icon. A painted image kept on a corner shelf, the thing grandmothers quietly guarded through the years when churches were shut and believers pressed.
Your line: the babushkas kept it. Lois, then Eunice, then Timothy. Day nine hundred seventy-one, done.

howItsDone: Orthodox homes may keep an icon corner with a lamp, and in some families grandparents teach children the prayers and the sign of the cross. Russian and other Orthodox churches now honor the new martyrs and confessors who suffered under Soviet rule.

chat.says: How did people in the Soviet Union keep their faith when the churches were closed?
options: Often through grandmothers: the icon corner, Easter bread, prayers taught in whispers.
Mostly through big public services the state allowed once a year, at Easter.
Mostly through priests who taught it openly in schools while officials looked away.
chat.meaning: In many stories from those years, babushkas kept faith alive at home: the icon corner, Easter bread, whispered prayers, like Timothy's grandmother Lois.
